children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
children.blurb: The AI enablement audit in an investment firm examines how artificial intelligence is introduced, approved, used, and monitored across the investment lifecycle.

children.name: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Fair lending and bias testing is the practice of checking whether credit decisions, pricing, marketing, and servicing treat applicants and borrowers fairly regardless of protected characteristics such as race, ethnicity, sex, age, or national origin.

children.name: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
children.blurb: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the practice of translating how an AI system reaches its outputs into language and evidence that non-specialists can assess.

children.name: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
children.blurb: Protecting material non-public information covers the rules and practices that keep confidential, price-sensitive facts about a company or its securities from being used in trading.

children.name: Verifying What a Model Produced
children.blurb: Verifying what a model produced means checking the output of an AI system against the purpose it was meant to serve, the sources it relied on, and the rules that apply to its use.

sections.body: Governance and fiduciary risk is the work of making AI use inside financial firms answerable to clients, regulators and internal policy. In practice, firms run enablement audits before teams adopt new tools, test credit and lending models for disparate impact, and write explanations that regulators and clients can follow. They also monitor communications and data flows to keep material non-public information from leaking into prompts or shared workspaces. When a model produces a summary, a recommendation or a number, staff are expected to verify it against source records rather than pass it along. This field is less about building models and more about controlling them, documenting them and proving that controls worked. The AI Economist treats it as part of the economics of AI because trust and compliance shape which tools can be deployed at scale.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work stands at a practical middle ground. Basic surveillance, access control and bias testing are routine in many firms, and vendors sell tools for each. What is not solved is deep explainability for large language models, causal proof that a model is fair, and reliable detection of sensitive data inside generative workflows. Audits are often point-in-time, bias tests depend on the quality of the data and the choice of metrics, and explanations can be plausible without being faithful to the model's actual reasoning. Verification of AI output remains a human review task in most settings, with sampling and escalation rather than full assurance. The site tracks 149 active AI lawsuits and 222 compliance and regulation pages, which reflects how much of this area is still being defined by enforcement, litigation and supervisory expectation.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section follow the control chain from readiness to output. The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms is the entry point for a firm asking whether a team, a tool or a workflow is ready for supervised use. Fair Lending and Bias Testing goes deeper into credit decisions, testing for disparate impact and documenting the results. Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients covers the written and spoken case for a model, including adverse action reasons and model risk documentation. Protecting Material Non-Public Information deals with confidentiality, prompt hygiene and surveillance of communications and data movement. Verifying What a Model Produced closes the loop with checks on citations, calculations, summaries and recommendations before they are relied on. A reader would go to the audit page for scope and controls, the fair lending page for credit testing, the explanation page for regulatory communication, the MNPI page for information barriers, and the verification page for output review.
